newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-ODD COUPLE READY TO FLY THE FLAG.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ODD COUPLE READY TO FLY THE FLAG.

text.p: It is tempting to imagine Tim Henman and Greg Rusedski as some sort of great British double act, as natural a pairing as, say, Lennon and McCartney or Torvill and Dean.

Both in the world's top 30, both dedicated professionals, both hungry for more. They each have girlfriends called Lucy and even share the same birthday, September 6. Anyone who has ever stood around waiting for a London bus will know how British tennis officials must be feeling.
Yet as Britain gapes at the possibility of two representatives in the Wimbledon semifinals, the twin pillars of an expectant nation's hopes are already beginning to shift uneasily.
It's just small things, of course, but in Britain it is those little details which matter.

Whereas Henman's family have sat impassively at courtside at all their son's matches, Tom and Helen Rusedski are back at home in Quebec. While Henman discusses his form in familiar English tones, Rusedski's accent remains stuck somewhere over the Atlantic. If Henman wins the title, there will be dancing in the streets of his home town, Oxford. If Rusedski wins, they will be sitting on their hands in Montreal.
Rusedski, a year older than Henman at 23, is resigned to such realities after adopting British nationality two years ago to the fury of Canada's tennis public.

His mother is from Dewsbury in Yorkshire, his girlfriend Lucy is English and he lives not far from Wimbledon in Putney, but while 'Henmania' has entered the English language, 'Rusedskimania' is stubbornly refusing to leave the launch-pad.
There were large numbers of empty seats on Court One for his fourth round match against American Richey Reneberg, in clear contrast to the packed Centre Court where Henman tackled Krajicek.

The left-handed Rusedski did his best to disguise the obvious conclusion -- "I guess they were all at lunch" -- yet must be privately wondering if he will ever escape the endless comparisons with the right-handed Henman.

He admits he is a tense personality, while Henman sat back on BBC television this week and acknowledged: "Fortunately I'm not someone who gets too nervous." Even world number one Pete Sampras has been struggling to be diplomatic.
"Mentally Tim's very, very strong. Even in the circus environment here, he's holding up very well," was the American top seed's verdict.
"Rusedski is a little bit more of a dangerous type of player, but Henman is very classical. I enjoy watching him play. He's going to be around for a lot of years."

Ask either man about the other and both tend to stare intently at their finger-tips. "I'm just focused on trying to get myself ready and I think Tim's the same way," said Rusedski, when asked if he planned to watch any of Henman's matches.

So as Henman reveals a sly humorous side -- "I think my Dad's growing greyer by the day...my family are complaining about the number of tie-breaks I'm playing" -- Rusedski increasingly appears on a hiding to nothing.
"If I get to the finals, I think my family would come the day after," he confessed. "My mother is superstitious. If she hasn't been here, she's not going to come until it's over."

Still, British tennis is not blase enough to ignore anyone capable of winning a grand slam final. Recent successes in rugby, cricket and soccer have sharpened the national appetite, and those who placed bets on a Briton winning Wimbledon before the end of the century are equally prepared to overlook the tiny detail that one of their men was born in Montreal.
"I'm sure I'll have a few more friends if that one comes up," acknowledges Rusedski.
"If it's 1,000-1 and you put 1,000 pounds on it, it's almost like winning the lottery."
His parents will not be the only ones staring anxiously at television sets in the coming days.
